questions.question: What are the three types of changes in ServiceNow?

explanation.correct: There are three types of changes in ServiceNow: Standard (pre-approved, commonly implemented), Normal (requires comprehensive assessments and CAB authorization), and Emergency (must be implemented swiftly, requires ECAB approval). See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: ServiceNow categorizes changes by type, not size.
Internal/External is not the classification used for change types.
These are not the official change type classifications in ServiceNow.

source.excerpt: There are three types of changes. When it comes to service changes, a normal change refers to any change that isn't classified as a standard change or an emergency change.

questions.question: What distinguishes a Standard change from a Normal change?

options.text: Standard changes cost more to implement
Standard changes are pre-approved and don't require CAB approval each time
Standard changes are only for emergency situations

explanation.correct: Standard changes are pre-approved, commonly implemented changes with established implementation steps and a track record of successful outcomes. Obtaining group-level or peer approval and CAB approval is not always necessary for standard changes. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Cost is not the distinguishing factor between change types.
Emergency changes are for urgent situations, not standard changes.
All change types are tracked in ServiceNow.

source.excerpt: Changes that are considered standard or pre-approved are commonly put into effect. These changes have a set of established implementation steps and a track record of successful outcomes.

questions.question: What does CAB stand for in Change Management?

explanation.correct: CAB stands for Change Advisory Board. Normal changes require comprehensive assessments and authorizations including peer or technical approval, Change Management, and Change Advisory Board authorization. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The correct term is Advisory, not Administration.
CAB relates to Change Management, not Configuration.
This is not the correct expansion of CAB.

source.excerpt: Such changes require comprehensive assessments and authorizations, including peer or technical approval, Change Management, and change advisory board authorization.

questions.question: What is the purpose of conflict detection in Change Management?

options.text: To detect scheduling conflicts with CIs, maintenance windows, and blackout periods
To find conflicts in change request descriptions

explanation.correct: The Change Management application helps identify schedule conflicts by analyzing factors such as configuration items, planned start and end dates, and change scope. Conflicts may arise from CI scheduling, maintenance windows, blackout windows, or assigned personnel availability. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: While personnel availability is checked, conflict detection covers much more.
Description conflicts are not what conflict detection analyzes.
Budget conflicts are handled separately from change conflict detection.

source.excerpt: The Change Management application helps identify schedule conflicts for change requests by analyzing factors such as configuration items, planned start and end dates, and change scope.

questions.question: What does the 'Authorized' state mean in the change lifecycle?

options.text: CAB has provided final authorization and we're waiting for the scheduled window

explanation.correct: Authorized means that CAB has provided the final authorization to proceed with the change, and we're simply waiting for the scheduled window. When the scheduled window occurs, it's time to implement the change. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Implementation happens after the Authorized state when the scheduled window arrives.
Canceled is a separate state from Authorized.
Assess is a different state where peer review is being conducted.

source.excerpt: Authorized means that CAB has provided the final authorization to proceed with the change, and we're simply waiting for the scheduled window.

questions.question: Why is it best practice to create emergency changes from an incident?

options.text: To minimize the risk of unauthorized changes by associating with a documented incident
To speed up the approval process automatically
Emergency changes cannot be created any other way

explanation.correct: Emergency changes do not follow the complete lifecycle of a normal change, which can potentially lead to unauthorized changes. To minimize this risk, it is best practice to create emergency changes if they are associated with an incident. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: The main reason is to minimize unauthorized changes, not reduce paperwork.
ECAB approval is still required; linking to incidents doesn't bypass approvals.
Emergency changes can be created independently, but linking is best practice.

source.excerpt: To be implemented swiftly, emergency changes do not follow the complete lifecycle of a normal change, which can potentially lead to unauthorized changes. To minimize this risk, it is best practice to create emergency changes if they are associated with an incident.

questions.question: What are the four types of change tasks in ServiceNow?

explanation.correct: ServiceNow offers four types of change tasks: Planning, Implementation, Testing, and Review tasks. Each task has states including pending, open, in progress, closed, and canceled. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: These are database operations, not change task types.
These are change states, not task types.
These are not the official change task type names.

source.excerpt: ServiceNow offers four types of change tasks-- namely, planning, implementation, testing, and review tasks.

questions.question: What is a change model in ServiceNow?

options.text: A template that defines the process, fields, states, approvals, and tasks for specific change types

explanation.correct: The process details, such as the specific fields, record states, approvals or pre-approvals, and tasks created are determined by the change model and change policies. Multimodal Change allows customization of activities and workflows for specific use cases. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Change models are process templates, not visualizations.
Cost estimation is handled separately from change models.
Database schemas are different from change models.

source.excerpt: The process details, such as the specific fields, record states, approvals or pre-approvals, and tasks created are determined by the change model and change policies.

questions.question: A change request has scheduling conflicts detected. What should the change owner do?

options.text: Ignore the conflicts and proceed immediately
Review conflicts and either amend the change to avoid them or document justification in work notes
Wait for the conflicts to resolve automatically

explanation.correct: It is up to the change owner or assigned user to review the conflicts and decide whether to amend the change to avoid conflicts or proceed anyway. Work notes should be constantly updated with justification if conflicts are ignored, as change approvers can also see them. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Ignoring conflicts without documentation is not best practice.
Cancellation may not be necessary if conflicts can be resolved or justified.
Conflicts don't resolve automatically; action is required.

source.excerpt: It is up to the change owner or the assigned to user to review the conflicts and decide whether to amend the change to avoid conflicts or proceed, anyway. We will constantly update the work notes with the justification if conflicts are ignored.

questions.question: Which methods are available for determining the risk of a change? (Choose two)

options.text: Risk assessments using end-user provided information

explanation.correct: There are two methods for determining change risk: risk conditions (using predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value) and risk assessments (relying on information provided by the end user). Both can be used independently or combined, with the highest risk value chosen. See: https://learning.servicenow.com/lxp/en/pages/learning-course?id=learning_course&course_id=f782895d93d09a5c56aeb94c5cba1044&child_id=ecb20dd947dc9a5089c7acc9126d4383&spa=1

wrongAnswers.explanation: Risk should be calculated systematically, not based solely on personal judgment.
Risk assignment is never random; it follows defined methods.

source.excerpt: To determine the risk of a change, there are two methods available. The first is through risk conditions, which utilize predefined properties and conditions to calculate a risk value. The second is through risk assessments, which rely on the information provided by the end user to assess a risk value.

questions.question: An update set has been marked as 'Complete' but additional changes are needed. What is the recommended approach?

options.text: Revert the update set back to 'In Progress' and make the changes
Create a new update set and commit them in the order they were created
Delete the completed update set and start over
Merge the changes directly into the default update set

explanation.correct: Once an update set is marked as complete, don't revert it back to in-progress. Instead, start a new update set and commit them in the order they were created. Use naming conventions like 'Performance Enhancements' and 'Performance Enhancements 2' to keep them organized.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Best practice is to NOT revert a completed update set back to in-progress.
Deleting a completed update set loses the captured changes. Create a new one instead.
The default update set should not be used for moving customizations between instances.

questions.question: How many instances does a ServiceNow customer receive at minimum?

explanation.correct: Customers receive at least two instances: production and non-production. They can add more for tasks like testing, development, or quality assurance.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Customers receive at least two instances, not one.
The minimum is two instances. Additional instances can be added but are not included by default.
Four instances are not the minimum; the minimum is two.

questions.question: What architecture does ServiceNow use for its instances?

explanation.correct: ServiceNow uses a multi-instance single-tenant architecture, meaning each instance has its own isolated database. Each instance is hosted at a ServiceNow data center with a unique URL.

wrongAnswers.explanation: ServiceNow is single-tenant (each customer has isolated instances), not multi-tenant.
ServiceNow provides multiple instances per customer (multi-instance) with single tenancy.
Customers receive multiple instances (at least 2), so it is multi-instance.

course.lessonTitle: Explore the power of the ServiceNow Platform

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Change Advisory Board (CAB) Workbench?

options.text: To automatically approve all change requests
To help CAB managers schedule and manage meetings to review and authorize change requests
To create new change request templates
To generate reports on historical change success rates

explanation.correct: The Change Advisory Board Workbench helps CAB managers schedule and manage meetings to review and authorize change requests.

wrongAnswers.explanation: The CAB Workbench facilitates review meetings; it doesn't automatically approve changes.
Change templates are created through the change management module, not the CAB Workbench.
While reporting is available, the primary purpose is managing CAB review meetings.

questions.question: When merging multiple update sets, how does ServiceNow handle conflicts where the same object was modified?

options.text: It keeps the latest change to the object
It prompts the admin to choose which version to keep
It creates a new version combining both changes

explanation.correct: When merging update sets, the latest change to an object is kept. This is why it's important to commit update sets in the order they were created.

wrongAnswers.explanation: The merge is not rejected; the system handles conflicts by keeping the latest change.
The system automatically keeps the latest change rather than prompting for selection.
ServiceNow doesn't merge the content of both changes; it keeps the latest one.

questions.question: What are the three types of change in ServiceNow's Change Management? (Choose 3)

explanation.correct: ServiceNow supports three change types: Standard (pre-approved, low-risk, repeatable), Normal (requires assessment and approval through the full change process), and Emergency (fast-tracked for urgent fixes to critical issues).

wrongAnswers.explanation: Cosmetic is not a standard change type in ServiceNow.
Routine is not a defined change type; Standard changes cover pre-approved routine activities.

questions.question: A change implementer discovers a critical issue during the implementation of a Normal change. The change cannot be completed as planned. What should be recorded?

options.text: Move the change to 'Review' state and document it as an unsuccessful implementation with rollback details
Delete the change record and create a new one
Close the change as successful anyway
Convert the change to an Emergency type

explanation.correct: Failed implementations should be documented by moving the change to Review state with details about what went wrong and the rollback steps taken. This maintains the audit trail and supports post-implementation review.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Deleting records destroys the audit trail; failed changes should be documented, not deleted.
Marking a failed change as successful compromises data integrity and makes future planning unreliable.
Converting to Emergency doesn't address the implementation failure; Emergency type is for urgent changes, not failed ones.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'Change Advisory Board' (CAB) in ServiceNow?

options.text: To review, assess, and approve or reject Normal and Emergency changes
To implement changes on behalf of the change owner

explanation.correct: The CAB is a group of stakeholders who review proposed changes for risk, impact, and scheduling conflicts. They provide approval or rejection decisions, particularly for Normal changes that require assessment.

wrongAnswers.explanation: The CAB reviews and approves changes; implementation is performed by the assigned team or implementer.
Scheduling is done by change coordinators; the CAB reviews and approves, they don't schedule.
Standard change templates are created by administrators, not typically by the CAB.

questions.question: Which feature helps prevent scheduling conflicts between changes affecting the same Configuration Item?

options.text: The Change Conflict detection feature that checks for overlapping change windows on the same CI
A UI Policy that prevents saving duplicate change records
The Assignment Rule that checks group workload
The SLA timer on the change record

explanation.correct: ServiceNow's Change Conflict detection (also called Change Collision) identifies scheduling overlaps when multiple changes target the same CI or related CIs during overlapping time windows, preventing conflicting changes.

wrongAnswers.explanation: UI Policies control form behavior; they don't detect scheduling conflicts.
Assignment Rules route tickets based on conditions; they don't check change schedule conflicts.
SLA timers track service level compliance, not scheduling conflicts.

questions.question: Which statement about Standard changes is NOT correct?

options.text: Standard changes are pre-approved and don't require CAB review each time
Standard changes use templates for consistent implementation
Standard changes require a new risk assessment for every request
Standard changes are low-risk, well-understood procedures

explanation.correct: Standard changes are pre-approved precisely because their risk has already been assessed and accepted. They do NOT require a new risk assessment each time — that would defeat the purpose of pre-approval.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Correct — Standard changes are pre-approved and skip CAB review.
Correct — Standard changes use templates to ensure consistency.
Correct — Standard changes are by definition low-risk and well-understood.
